The prognosis for patients with allergic contact dermatitis appears to be influenced by several factors, including the omnipresence of the allergen. A two-year follow-up survey of patients with this condition from an occupational cohort found that those who experienced contact urticaria had a poorer prognosis than those who had contact allergy.

Furthermore, there was a trend towards a poorer prognosis for those with contact allergy to rubber chemicals compared to those with allergy to epoxy. This suggests that the severity and prevalence of allergic reactions may be related to the specific allergens present in an individual's environment.

It is also worth noting that patients undergoing job changes experienced improvements in their condition, indicating that changing jobs can lead to a reduction in symptoms. This implies that environmental factors play a role in the development and severity of allergic contact dermatitis.

Overall, these findings suggest that the prognosis for patients with allergic contact dermatitis may be influenced by various factors, including the omnipresence of allergens and changes in environmental exposure during job changes.
